meta.subject: Geography
meta.title: Physical Features of India
meta.intro: The geological structure and six major physiographic divisions of India, including the Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains and Islands.

objectives: Explain physical features of india using geographical concepts and Indian examples.
Identify the important terms, patterns, processes and locations in this chapter.
Interpret maps, tables and geographical evidence.
Connect the chapter with human life, environment and regional development.

blocks.text: India’s present relief is the result of long geological processes. The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient, stable landmass, while the Himalayas are young fold mountains formed by the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate.

The Indian Plate moved northwards after breaking away from the ancient southern supercontinent Gondwanaland. Its collision with the Eurasian Plate compressed sediments and uplifted the Himalayan mountain system.
The description and study of the surface features of the Earth, such as mountains, plateaus, plains and valleys.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.text: India’s major landforms differ in age, structure, height, origin and geological stability.
The Himalayas form a geologically young and lofty mountain system along India’s northern boundary. They extend in an arc from the Indus gorge in the west to the Brahmaputra gorge in the east.

The Himalayas are commonly divided into three parallel ranges. Himadri or Greater Himalaya is the northernmost and highest range, with permanently snow-covered peaks and glaciers. Himachal or Lesser Himalaya lies south of it and includes ranges such as the Pir Panjal. Shiwalik is the outermost and lowest range.
Longitudinal valleys between the Lesser Himalaya and Shiwalik are called duns. Dehradun is a well-known example.
The eastern extension of the Himalayas is known as the Purvachal. It includes the Patkai, Naga, Manipur and Mizo hills, which curve along India’s northeastern boundary.

The Northern Plains were formed by the deposition of alluvium brought by the Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries. They are extensive, level and fertile, making them important for agriculture, transport and dense settlement.
The plains are often divided into the Punjab Plains, Ganga Plains and Brahmaputra Plains. Their local relief includes the Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar and Khadar belts.
A narrow, porous belt of pebbles and coarse sediments along the foothills where streams often disappear underground.
A marshy, wet belt south of the Bhabar where streams re-emerge and the ground is waterlogged in many places.
Older alluvium found above the floodplains, often containing calcareous concretions called kankar.
Newer alluvium deposited by rivers in active floodplains and renewed by periodic floods.

blocks.title: Bhangar vs Khadar
blocks.text: Bhangar is older alluvium on slightly higher terraces; Khadar is newer alluvium in lower floodplain areas.
The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient tableland made mainly of crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks. It is roughly triangular and is one of the oldest landmasses of the Indian subcontinent.
The Central Highlands lie north of the Narmada River and include the Malwa Plateau and adjoining uplands. The Deccan Plateau lies south of the Narmada and is bounded by the Western and Eastern Ghats.
The Western Ghats are generally higher and more continuous than the Eastern Ghats. The Eastern Ghats are discontinuous and are cut by rivers flowing towards the Bay of Bengal.
The Chotanagpur Plateau is known for mineral resources, while the Deccan Trap region contains extensive basaltic lava formations and black soil in many areas.

sections.title: Indian Desert, Coastal Plains and Islands

blocks.text: The Indian Desert lies mainly west of the Aravalli Hills. It has very low rainfall, sandy plains and shifting sand dunes. The Luni is an important river of this region.

The western coastal plain is a narrow strip between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea. It includes the Konkan, Kannad and Malabar coasts. The eastern coastal plain is broader in many stretches and includes the Northern Circars and Coromandel Coast; large rivers form deltas here.

India has two major island groups. Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea is of coral origin. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal and include strategically important island chains; Barren Island has an active volcano.
